Neha / all — see two proposed drafting blocks below. I also attached a short matrix showing examples of when lost profits are likely to be treated as direct (integration/order failure that prevents revenue capture) versus indirect/consequential (marketwide opportunity loss, reputational harm).

Option A — Customer-Focused (redlines to keep recoverability narrow):
"""
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Agreement, either party's liability for damages shall be limited to direct, provable damages arising from the non-breaching party's actual, out-of-pocket loss resulting directly from a breach of this Agreement, subject to the cap set forth in Section X. For the avoidance of doubt, recoverable direct damages may include reasonable, documented costs incurred to restore Customer data and fees for lost orders attributable to a proven failure of the Service to process Customer transactions when such failure is temporally and causally linked to the Services provided hereunder. Consequential, incidental, special, punitive or exemplary damages (including, without limitation, lost profits, loss of business opportunities, loss of goodwill and losses arising from customers' customers) are excluded.
"""

Option B — Compromise (business-friendly limitation for data/IP breaches):
"""
Notwithstanding the foregoing, in the event of a breach resulting in unauthorized access to or loss of Customer data, Redwood's liability shall include documented, reasonable costs to restore Customer data and, solely for the purpose of such data-loss incidents, proven lost transaction fees directly resulting from the Service outage, subject to an aggregate sub-cap equal to two (2) times the fees paid by Customer for the three (3) months preceding the incident. All other categories of consequential damages (including, but not limited to, loss of business, loss of goodwill and punitive damages) remain excluded.
"""

Business impact notes:
- Option A keeps overall exposure constrained and ties lost profits recovery to narrow, provable order-processing failures only.
- Option B concedes a limited, quantified sub-cap for data incidents to help bridge with large enterprise customers; the sub-cap is time-bound and tied to fee history to keep predictability.

I recommend we propose Option B to Acme first — they are large and public-facing; giving a controlled data incident concession reduces procurement pushback while preserving a firm boundary on broader consequential losses.

— Marcus

Marcus — good drafts. A couple of quick edits and procurement considerations:

1) Wording tweak: change 'proven lost transaction fees' to 'documented lost transaction fees' (proof standard can become litigious; we should ask for contemporaneous logs).
2) If we include the two-times-three-month sub-cap, procurement will likely ask for a longer lookback (6 months) or a higher multiplier. We should be prepared with rationale for using three months: it keeps exposure proportional and aligns with invoicing cycles.
3) If Acme insists on lost profits outside data incidents, push for a carve-in only where loss is directly traceable to a Service outage affecting specific transaction flows (and require demonstrable attribution).

Operational ask: Marcus, can you add a one-line fallback that requires both parties to engage in commercially reasonable mitigation steps (including using backups and recovery playbooks) before claiming restoration fees? That will help reduce speculative claims.

Happy to review final reply before we send.

— Laura
Laura Bennett
Head of Procurement Programs
Redwood Inference

Samantha/Tom — thanks for the clear note and the redlines. We reviewed internally and propose the following compromise language (attached as a tracked-change snippet in the MSA file) along the lines of Option B below. Short summary below and attached rationale for your counsel.

Summary (one paragraph): Redwood is willing to permit documented restoration costs and documented lost transaction fees that are directly attributable to a Service outage affecting order processing, subject to an incident-specific sub-cap equal to two (2) times the Customer's fees for the three (3) months preceding the incident. All other categories of consequential damages, including loss of business, loss of goodwill and general lost profits not directly traceable to an identified service failure, remain excluded. Parties must follow commercially reasonable mitigation steps (including use of backups and playbooks) before recovery.

Next steps:
- We attached the redline (Acme_MSA_Redlines_v3.docx) with the tracked change and a short examples PDF that maps 'lost transaction' vs 'lost profit' scenarios.
- If you're happy with the text, we can have legal prepare a final MSA for signature early next week.
- If Acme legal prefers to propose a longer lookback or higher multiplier (e.g., 6 months or 3x fees), let's schedule a 30-min call to negotiate tradeoffs (pricing or SLA credits).

Appreciate the quick turnaround — happy to jump on a call if helpful.

Best,
Neha Kapoor
VP, Revenue Operations
